title: Designing Better UI Filter Systems
summary: This lesson explains how to design effective filter chips by managing states, logic, and mobile layouts. It emphasizes immediate feedback, clear exit strategies, and maintaining visibility of active filters to improve user experience.

transcript.text: A chip lives in three states: idle, active, disabled.
If active looks like idle, the filter feels broken.
Pick two colors and results grow. Add a size and they shrink.
Or within a group and across the groups. More chips in one group widen the net. A new group narrows it.
Every tap needs an answer. Update the result count the moment a chip flips.
Stacked filters trap people in a corner. One clear-all button resets the set.
Pair it with a count so they know what it wipes. Always leave an exit.
10 chips never fit a phone. Scroll them sideways in one row.
Fade the edge so users feel there is more. Wrapping into a wall buries the results.
Filters out of sight get forgotten. Keep the active ones pinned on top.
Users should see why the list shrank.
Follow for more UI systems. Save this for your next product page.

on_screen_text: Idle: Surface + border. Tappable, not chosen.
Active: Teal fill + check. Clearly selected.
Disabled: Dimmed. No results behind it.
design_principles: State differentiation (Idle vs Active vs Disabled)
Boolean logic (OR within groups, AND across groups)
Mobile space optimization (Horizontal scroll vs wrapping)
Visibility of system status (Pinned active filters)
before_after: Demonstrates the transition from wrapping chips into a 'wall' that hides results to using a single horizontal scrolling row with an edge fade to preserve screen real estate.
